brief: A top-down view looks into a garden bed of curly lacinato and red kale at dawn after the first frost. The scene is drawn in coloured pencil on toned blue-grey paper. The leaves are deep slate-green and plum-violet, and every crinkle is outlined by needle-fine white pencil crystals. Feathery hoarfrost fronds grow along the leaf ribs, and dark, frost-free shadows sit where leaves overlap. The surrounding soil is dusted with pale rime. The light is cold and sourceless, and the palette is restrained. Precise, burnished layers make the ice look brittle enough to snap.

A commuter's hand grips a train hanging-strap, cropped hard at the top-left corner. Through the window behind, the sky is a flat bokashi gradient from Prussian blue to pale bone, with a tiny snow-capped Fuji sitting low. The hand is fiercely hyperreal: knuckle creases, a vein, a plaster on one finger, the worn sheen of the plastic ring. Crisp fine-pen keylines trace the strap and window frame in woodblock fashion, while the skin is modelled in soft graded washes. Strong asymmetric diagonals and calm flatness make it read as a Hiroshige view caught on a phone.

Three hyperreal blocks of silken tofu sit on a damp cedar board, lit only by light diffused through paper. The values are very high-key: ivory, rice-white and the faintest warm grey. Soft graphite with smudged tonal gradation renders the tofu's trembling, slightly glossy skin and its tiny pores. Pale watercolour glazes give the cedar its blush of salmon-pink. A faint lattice of light falls across everything, barely perceptible, like the memory of a grid. Almost nothing is dark. The atmosphere is hushed, muted and enveloping, a study in near-white form.

One enormous hyperreal tomato slice is cropped so that only a curving arc fills the whole picture edge to edge. The scale is a bold 1960s textile print blown up to fabric width. Large expanses of flesh are confident flat marker fields of carmine and cadmium red, laid in broad, slightly overlapping swaths. Inside the seed chambers the realism sharpens hard: glassy gel, pale seeds, a white fibrous core, and wet highlights in fine pencil and pen. A single band of cream background peeks in at one corner. It is graphic, joyous and oversized.

A low horizon and an enormous sky. On a rocky ridge stands a hyperreal cairn of smooth, wet-dark slate pebbles, each stone stacked like a lens. Above it hovers a stack of lenticular clouds, smooth-edged saucers layered in pale peach, lavender-grey and cold white. The sky and clouds are soft spray gradients with no visible strokes, glassy and still. The cairn is coloured pencil over spray, picking out mica glints, lichen specks and water sheen on the stone. The stacked forms rhyme vertically, small and near against huge and far. The mood is calm, airless and enormous.

A length of freshly dyed cotton thrown over pale sand dunes to dry, filling the frame with heavy folds. Deep indigo and madder-red watercolour is laid in saturated layers. Crisp reserved white and black lines form a block-printed geometric lattice, which bends and compresses accurately over each fold, crease and sagging hollow. Rows of tiny stars are held back as bare paper. The resist edges show a faint crackle bleed. Sand grains are scattered on the cloth in fine pencil stipple. Hard sun throws deep, cool shadows into the troughs.

A hyperreal view down a sandstone stepwell. Zigzag flights of stairs drop in stacked, mirrored tiers toward a dark green pool, and a single dented brass lota sits on one landing. The medium is hard graphite with dense, controlled cross-hatching for every chisel scar and worn tread. Thin sepia and raw-sienna watercolour glazes go over it only where stone catches light. Toward the bottom the drawing falls into near-black graphite mass. The composition is vertigo-tight and geometric, with no sky. The brass lota is the only polished, reflective surface, its rim and dents rendered almost photographically.

A hyperreal raw salmon fillet lies on crinkled, translucent tan pattern tissue printed with black dashed cutting lines. The tissue also carries grain arrows, notches and faded part numbers. The fillet's printed outline almost matches the fish but drifts slightly off it. The salmon is layered watercolour and pencil in coral, apricot and silvery white marbling, with wet sheen and the cut grain of its flesh. The tissue's wrinkles and see-through overlaps are rendered in faint graphite. The view is flat-lay from above. The tone is clinical and slightly uncanny, food and garment logic overlaid.

A hyperreal cracked walnut, shell halves splayed to reveal the brain-like kernel, sits enthroned inside a painted Romanesque arch on squat columns. The arch and border are flat, saturated marker fields of lapis blue, vermilion and leaf-green with heavy black pen contours. The walnut breaks that flat world. Its shell ridges, papery membrane and oily kernel sheen are rendered in meticulous coloured pencil and fine pen stippling. A narrow band of stylised rinceau runs along the bottom. The tension of the piece is solemn medieval flatness against an obsessively real nut.

A teeming hyperreal heap of glass bangles fills the frame densely, with no empty space. The bangles come in every truck-art colour: emerald, hot pink, saffron, ultramarine and gold-flecked black. They lie tangled on a mirrored chamak-patti panel of reflective tape. Each bangle carries sharp specular streaks and refracted colour reflected in the bangles beside it. They are painted with saturated marker over watercolour, with crisp white pen glints and tiny fractured reflections. The border is a dense frame of painted petals and chevrons. The whole is loud, glittering and celebratory.

Out of deep velvety charcoal black, three black-gloved hands emerge holding up a hyperreal jointed wooden mannequin hand. Its fingers are articulated mid-gesture and its joints show pins and worn varnish. The mannequin hand is the only lit form, drawn in warm pencil and pale watercolour. Beech grain, scuffs and the glossy wear on its knuckles are rendered with tender exactness. The puppeteers' gloves are barely distinguishable from the void, their charcoal mass breaking up only at a crease. It reads as a theatrical, hushed piece about being manipulated.

A hyperreal halved red cabbage, its cut face a labyrinth of violet and white veins, lies off-centre on a flat gold-ochre field. The ground is built from laid, faintly seamed rectangles like gold-leaf squares. The cabbage's outer leaves are painted with pooled watercolour in the tarashikomi manner: wet indigo and magenta bloom into each other and leave dark, granulated tide-lines. The cut face is drawn in razor-fine pen with photographic precision. Bold asymmetry leaves a vast empty gold expanse to the right. The palette is Prussian blue, cobalt violet and burnished ochre. The feeling is luxurious and decorative, yet botanically exact.

A hyperreal photograph-like study of a black folded Scherenschnitte cutting, perhaps a symmetrical tree of birds and hearts. It lies slightly lifted and curling on a honey-coloured pine tabletop. The paper is matte carbon-black ink fill, with the faint crease of its central fold catching a dull grey highlight. Its cut edges show tiny feathered fibres in sharp pencil. Pine grain, knots and a soft contact shadow are rendered in warm watercolour washes. The view is overhead and slightly raking. The craft object itself is the subject, rendered so precisely that you feel the paper's thinness.

A single hyperreal ear of multicoloured flint corn, husks peeled back, fills the frame diagonally. Everything is built from tightly packed parallel lines that follow each contour, like yarn pressed into wax. Each kernel is a nest of concentric marker strokes in fuchsia, turquoise, saffron and blood-orange, with a tiny glossy highlight left bare. The background is concentric lines too, rippling outward in cobalt and acid lime. No surface is filled flat: every inch is line. The ear stays volumetric and fully believable, as if photographed and then re-threaded.

A hyperreal slab of thick lake ice, lifted and propped upright, shows a jade-grey-green depth like celadon glaze. Inside it, columns of trapped bubbles and a fine web of crackle fractures catch the light. The medium is many layered translucent watercolour glazes in pale celadon, grey-blue and milky white, building real depth. A hairline pen network traces the crackle, darkening where fractures overlap. The background is a muted, cool grey wash. The composition is calm, nearly frontal and restrained. The surface should feel cold, glassy and quietly precious.

An all-over scatter of tiny hyperreal pulses on soft powder-pink cotton lawn: red lentils, green split peas, black beluga lentils and olive mung beans. They are spaced evenly in a dense ditsy repeat with no focal point. Each is drawn in coloured pencil at a tiny scale, with its own highlight, seed scar and miniature cast shadow. The cloth beneath shows a faint woven texture and a gentle diagonal fold across the sheet. The palette is sweet and nostalgic, like a dress print. Only a close look reveals that these are real, edible grains.

An overhead view of round tandir flatbreads laid in a strict lattice on a deep madder-red cloth. Each loaf is stamped with an octagonal gul-like pattern of pricked dots and stepped borders. The breads are hyperreal: blistered crust, charred spots and sesame seeds, built from dense cross-hatching in burnt sienna, ochre and soot black. The gaps between loaves form secondary diamond motifs in indigo and ivory. The repetition is rigorous but every loaf differs slightly. It is warm, abundant and architectonic.

An oblique bird's-eye view of a small island ferry harbour, rendered hyperreal yet laid out like a pictorial tourist map. The tilted perspective flattens toward the horizon. Every bollard, rooftop tile, moored dinghy and café umbrella is drawn in crisp sepia pen. Clear watercolour fills follow in Prussian blue sea, terracotta roofs and sage scrub. A ferry trails a wake of fine curling lines. Tiny cartouche-like blank banners float over key buildings. The whole sheet is full-bleed and busy, cheerful and inviting.

A hyperreal frontal portrait of a moth's head, with feathered antennae, compound eyes and furry thorax. It is presented as though imaged in separate stained channels on pure black. The scales are in cyan, the antennae filaments in hot magenta and the eyes in acid-free emerald green, with overlaps blending toward white. The rendering is fine-tipped pen and layered marker, with every scale an individual crisp mark. It is surgically centred like a lab plate yet monumental in scale. It feels scientific, intimate and alien.

A hyperreal low-angle view into the intake of a parked jet engine on a hot tarmac apron. The titanium fan blades spiral inward in razor-sharp pen linework over graphite tone. A single horizontal flare slices the whole frame edge to edge in electric cyan and pale violet, laid in soft airbrushed spray with oval ghost reflections strung along it. The edges are cinematic and letterboxed: heavy unpainted bands top and bottom, and the asphalt heat shimmer is rendered in faint streaked marker. The piece feels like a frozen film still with a clinical, expensive, wide-screen hush.
